name_en: Gu Shu Dian Hong (Ancient-Tree Yunnan Black)
cultivar: Seed-grown old arbor trees of Yunnan large-leaf (assamica) populations
processing: Fully oxidised black tea from old-tree leaf: withered, rolled, oxidised and dried; makers often oxidise slightly less than plantation Dian Hong and some finish with sun-drying rather than hot air.
harvest_season: Spring (late March to April) is what the price is paid for; autumn old-tree black exists and is softer and cheaper.
appearance_dry: Large, thick, loosely twisted dark leaves with only a few golden tips, less uniform than plantation tea.
appearance_liquor: Deep amber-orange, very clear, darkening to red as the steeps lengthen.
appearance_wet: Big, thick, leathery copper-brown leaves with long stems.
taste_profile: Dried apricot, honey and wild flowers over a stony, mineral clarity, with a sweetness that returns in the throat long after swallowing; little or no sweet-potato note.

brewing.notes: Brew it like a good sheng: water near the boil, short steeps, and be patient with the late infusions, which is where this tea beats plantation Dian Hong. It does not turn bitter.

vintage_note: Sold by village and spring harvest year, often as loose leaf but also pressed into cakes or dragon balls. Unlike ordinary Dian Hong it is routinely kept: good lots improve for two or three years as the fruit deepens, and sun-dried versions are stored longer still. Most of what is on sale is the current or previous year's spring.
description:
Gu shu Dian Hong is Yunnan black made from old, seed-grown tea trees – the same 'ancient tree' material that raw pu-erh drinkers chase, processed as black tea instead. It is a recent market style rather than an old one, though no known source dates it; the usual seller's story is that Yunnan makers realised that old-tree leaf, which is less tippy and fuzzy than plantation bush leaf, could sell on depth of flavour rather than looks. It is the least typical Dian Hong and the one most worth seeking out if sweet potato is not your thing.

The leaf comes from trees in Lincang (Fengqing, Yongde, Mengku), Baoshan, Jinggu and parts of Xishuangbanna that are usually claimed to be a century or more old; 'da shu' (big tree) is the more honest label for mature trees of unknown age. Processing is standard black tea – withering, rolling, oxidation, drying – but makers often oxidise a little less and some dry in the sun (shai hong), both of which keep the finish long and alive.

The cup is the point: dried apricot, honey and wild flowers rather than baked potato, a mineral, almost stony clarity, and a sweetness that comes back in the throat long after you swallow. It also goes ten steeps or more. Brew it like a good sheng: 5–6 g in a gaiwan, water near the boil, short steeps; it does not turn bitter and rewards patience in the late infusions.

It is sold by village and spring harvest year, priced well above regular Dian Hong, and the 'gu shu' claim is unregulated. Judge it by the leaf – large, thick, loosely twisted, few tips – and by whether the late steeps still have flavour, which is where plantation tea gives up. Many are pressed into cakes or dragon balls, and good ones improve for two or three years.

If you drink sheng pu-erh, this is the black tea most likely to convince you.
history:
The parent tea has a clear start: Dian Hong dates from 1938 and 1939, when Feng Shaoqiu made trial black tea in Shunning, now Fengqing, and the name itself was fixed in 1940. Old-tree black tea is a much later and much vaguer thing. No known source dates it or names who started it, so read it as a recent market style, not a historic tea.

What is documented is mostly selling language. Shops describe the leaf as coming from old arbor trees, sometimes with very large ages attached, and those ages have no independent check behind them. Treat "gu shu" as a seller's claim and "da shu" as the more modest version of it.
